l: heavens and the earth, Genesis, Chapter 2
s: The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array are described as finished, and the text calls the account the history of the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created. Before plants appeared and before there was a man to till the ground, a mist watered the ground, and the LORD God then formed man, the garden's trees, the animals, and the woman.

The serpent, the most subtle of the animals, persuades the woman to eat the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden by denying that she will die and promising she will be like God. The woman eats and gives some to her husband, and both realize they are naked and sew fig leaves as coverings. When the LORD God walks in the garden and questions them, the man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent. The LORD God then pronounces curses on the serpent, the woman, and Adam, and the man names his wife Eve. The LORD God clothes them in animal skins and sends the man out of the garden of Eden, placing cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

The LORD God walks in the garden, calls to the man, and questions the man and the woman about what they have done. He pronounces curses on the serpent, the woman, and Adam, makes garments of animal skins to clothe Adam and his wife, and observes that the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. He sends the man out of Eden and places cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

The serpent, described as more subtle than any animal of the field, questions the woman about God's command and tells her she won't really die, and that her eyes will be opened and she will be like God. When confronted, the woman says it deceived her. The LORD God curses it above all livestock and animals, condemning it to go on its belly and eat dust, and sets hostility between its offspring and the woman's offspring, who will bruise its head while it bruises his heel.

The woman answers the serpent, restating God's command and adding that they must not touch the fruit. She sees that the tree is good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable for wisdom, eats its fruit, and gives some to her husband. She says the serpent deceived her, is told she will have greatly multiplied pain in childbirth and that her husband will rule over her, and is named Eve by the man because she will be the mother of all the living.

Adam eats the fruit his wife gives him, then hides from the LORD God, saying he was afraid because he was naked. He blames the woman whom God gave him. He is told the ground is cursed for his sake, that he will eat with much labor, from thorns and thistles, by the sweat of his face until he returns to dust, and he is sent out of the garden to till the ground from which he was taken.

The garden is the setting where the serpent tempts the woman, the couple hide among its trees, and the LORD God walks in the cool of the day. The man is sent out of it to till the ground. Cherubim and a flaming sword that turns every way are placed at its east to guard the way to the tree of life.

l: tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Genesis, Chapter 3
s: The tree in the middle of the garden is the one whose fruit God forbade eating or touching on pain of death. The woman sees it as good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise, and its fruit is eaten by her and then the man. The serpent claims eating it will open their eyes so they know good and evil like God, and God later confirms the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.

l: eating the forbidden fruit (the Fall), Genesis, Chapter 3
s: The woman eats the fruit after the serpent's persuasion and gives some to her husband, who also eats. Their eyes are opened and they know they are naked, so they sew fig leaves for coverings and hide from God. The act leads God to question them, pronounce curses, and send the man out of the garden.

The serpent is cursed above all livestock and animals, to go on its belly and eat dust, with hostility between its offspring and the woman's. The woman is given greatly multiplied pain in childbirth, desire for her husband, and his rule over her. Adam faces cursed ground, laborious eating with thorns and thistles, bread by the sweat of his face, and return to dust, and the man is driven out of the garden away from the tree of life.

Eve gives birth to Cain and then Abel, a tiller of the ground and a keeper of sheep respectively. The LORD respects Abel's offering but not Cain's, and despite the LORD's warning that sin crouches at the door, Cain kills Abel in the field. The LORD curses Cain to be a fugitive and wanderer, marks him with a sign so no one will strike him, and Cain settles in the land of Nod, where he fathers Enoch and builds a city. Cain's descendants include Lamech, whose sons Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal Cain become founders of herding, music, and metalworking, and who boasts of killing a man and of being avenged seventy-seven times. Adam and Eve have another son, Seth, whose son Enosh is born as men begin to call on the LORD's name.

Cain, a tiller of the ground, brings an offering that the LORD does not respect, becomes angry, and kills his brother Abel in the field. He is cursed to be a fugitive and wanderer, given a protective sign, and settles in Nod, where he has a son Enoch, builds a city named for him, and becomes the ancestor of Lamech's line.

Abel, Cain's brother and a keeper of sheep, brings the firstborn of his flock and its fat, and the LORD respects him and his offering. Cain kills him in the field, and his blood cries out to the LORD from the ground; Eve later names Seth as another child in his place.

The LORD respects Abel's offering but not Cain's, warns Cain about sin, and confronts him after the killing. He curses Cain, promises sevenfold vengeance on anyone who slays him, and appoints a sign for him. By the end, men begin to call on the LORD's name.

Eve, wife of the man, conceives and gives birth to Cain, saying she has gotten a man with the LORD's help, and then to Abel. She later bears Seth, saying God has given her another child instead of Abel, whom Cain killed.

Lamech, Cain's descendant through Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, and Methushael, takes two wives, Adah and Zillah, and is father of Jabal, Jubal, Tubal Cain, and a daughter Naamah. He tells his wives he has slain a young man for wounding him and claims that if Cain is avenged seven times, he will be avenged seventy-seven times.
The LORD tells Cain that sin crouches at the door, that its desire is for him, and that he is to rule over it. Cain then kills Abel.

Cain invites Abel into the field, rises up against him, and kills him. The LORD confronts Cain, says Abel's blood cries from the ground, and curses Cain to be a fugitive and wanderer, though he also appoints a sign to protect him.

Chapter 5 presents the book of the generations of Adam, recording that God made man in his own likeness and named them Adam. It traces the line from Adam through Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, and Lamech to Noah, giving each man's age at the birth of his heir, the years he lived afterward, and his total lifespan. Each man except Enoch is said to have died. Enoch walked with God and was not found, for God took him. The chapter ends with Lamech naming Noah, who at age five hundred became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

Adam was made by God in God's likeness, and God created them male and female, blessed them, and named them Adam. He lived 130 years and fathered Seth in his own likeness, after his image. He then lived 800 more years, fathered other sons and daughters, and died at 930.
God created man in his own likeness, made them male and female, blessed them, and named them Adam. He is the one Enoch walked with, and he took Enoch so that Enoch was not found.
Seth was born to Adam in Adam's likeness and image. He lived 105 years before fathering Enosh, then 807 more years with other sons and daughters, and died at 912.
Enosh was born to Seth. He lived 90 years before fathering Kenan, then 815 more years with other sons and daughters, and died at 905.
Kenan was born to Enosh. He lived 70 years before fathering Mahalalel, then 840 more years with other sons and daughters, and died at 910.
Mahalalel was born to Kenan. He lived 65 years before fathering Jared, then 830 more years with other sons and daughters, and died at 895.
Jared was born to Mahalalel. He lived 162 years before fathering Enoch, then 800 more years with other sons and daughters, and died at 962.

Enoch was born to Jared and fathered Methuselah at 65. He walked with God for 300 years afterward and fathered more sons and daughters. His days totaled 365 years, and he was not found, for God took him.
Methuselah was born to Enoch. He lived 187 years before fathering Lamech, then 782 more years with other sons and daughters, and died at 969.

Lamech was born to Methuselah and fathered a son at 182, naming him Noah. He said Noah would comfort them in their work and toil caused by the ground the LORD cursed. He lived 595 more years with other sons and daughters and died at 777.

Noah was born to Lamech, who named him in hope that he would comfort them in their work and the toil of their hands, caused by the cursed ground. At age 500 Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

The chapter opens by calling itself the book of the generations of Adam. It records the line from Adam to Noah's sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, with each man's age at his heir's birth, years afterward, and total lifespan.

As men multiplied on the ground, God's sons took wives from among men's daughters, the Nephilim appeared, and the LORD declared that man's days would be one hundred twenty years. The LORD saw that man's wickedness was great and that every thought of his heart was continually evil, and he grieved and resolved to destroy man, animals, creeping things, and birds. Noah, a righteous and blameless man who walked with God and had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, found favor with the LORD. God, seeing the earth corrupt and filled with violence, told Noah he would end all flesh with a flood, and gave detailed instructions to build a ship of gopher wood, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high. God promised a covenant with Noah and told him to bring his family, two of every kind of creature, and food into the ship, and Noah did all that God commanded.

The LORD declared that his Spirit would not strive with man forever and limited man's days to one hundred twenty years. He saw that man's wickedness was great, was sorry and grieved that he had made man, and resolved to destroy man and the animals, creeping things, and birds, while Noah found favor in his eyes.

God saw that the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and told Noah he would end all flesh and destroy them and the earth. He commanded Noah to build a ship with specific dimensions, promised to establish his covenant with him, and instructed him to bring his family, two of every sort of creature, and food aboard.

Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes and is described as a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, who walked with God. He was father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and he did all that God commanded him, including preparing to build the ship.

Men multiplied on the ground and had daughters, whom God's sons took as wives. Their wickedness was great, with every thought of their hearts continually only evil, and the LORD resolved to destroy them, limiting their days to one hundred twenty years.

God announced that he would bring the flood of waters on the earth to destroy all flesh having the breath of life from under the sky. Everything on the earth would die, apart from those kept alive in the ship.

God commanded Noah to make the ship of gopher wood, with rooms, sealed inside and outside with pitch. It was to be three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high, with a roof finished to a cubit upward, a door in its side, and lower, second, and third levels.
The earth was corrupt before God and filled with violence, because all flesh had corrupted their way on it. God said he would destroy the earth along with all flesh, and bring a flood on it.

l: animals (creatures to be saved), Genesis, Chapter 6
s: The LORD first resolved to destroy animals, creeping things, and birds along with man. God then told Noah to bring two of every sort, male and female, of birds, livestock, and creeping things into the ship to keep them alive, along with food for them.

The LORD saw that man's wickedness was great and that every thought of his heart was continually only evil. The earth was corrupt and filled with violence, which became the reason God resolved to bring an end to all flesh.

The LORD tells Noah to enter the ship with his household because he has seen Noah's righteousness, and instructs him to take seven pairs of every clean animal and of the birds and two of each unclean animal, warning that rain will fall for forty days and forty nights after seven days. Noah obeys, and at age six hundred he enters the ship with his sons, wife, and sons' wives, along with the animals that come in pairs, and the LORD shuts him in. On the seventeenth day of the second month the fountains of the great deep burst open and the sky's windows open, and rain falls for forty days. The rising waters lift the ship and cover even the highest mountains by fifteen cubits. Every living thing on dry land dies, including people, livestock, creeping things, and birds, and only Noah and those with him in the ship are left as the waters flood the earth for one hundred fifty days.

Noah is told by the LORD to enter the ship with his household because of his righteousness, and he does everything the LORD commands. At age six hundred he goes into the ship with his family and the animals, and the LORD shuts him in. He and those with him are the only ones left alive after the flood destroys all other life on the earth.

The LORD commands Noah to enter the ship with his household and to bring clean and unclean animals and birds, citing Noah's righteousness. He announces that he will send rain for forty days and forty nights to destroy every living thing he has made, and he shuts Noah in the ship. The text also describes the animals going in as God's command.

The flood begins after seven days, when the fountains of the great deep burst open and the sky's windows open on the seventeenth day of the second month in Noah's six hundredth year. Rain falls for forty days and forty nights, and the waters rise until they cover all the high mountains by fifteen cubits. The waters flood the earth for one hundred fifty days and destroy all life on dry land except what is in the ship.

Noah, his household, and pairs of animals and birds enter the ship, and the LORD shuts them in. As the waters increase, the ship is lifted up above the earth and floats on the surface of the waters. Those inside it are the only survivors.

l: Noah's family (Noah's wife, sons and sons' wives), Genesis, Chapter 7
s: Noah's household, consisting of his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, his wife, and the three wives of his sons, enters the ship on the same day as Noah. They are included in the LORD's command to come into the ship. They survive the flood with Noah as those who were with him in the ship.

Clean and unclean animals, birds, livestock, and creeping things go into the ship by pairs, male and female, after their kinds, as God commanded; seven pairs of clean animals and of birds are to be taken to keep seed alive. All flesh on the earth and dry land that had the breath of life, including every man, dies in the flood. Only those in the ship with Noah are left.

God remembers Noah and the animals in the ship and sends a wind over the earth, stopping the fountains of the deep and the windows of the sky so the waters recede. The ship comes to rest on Ararat's mountains in the seventh month, and the mountain tops appear in the tenth month. Noah sends out a raven and then a dove three times; the dove returns with an olive leaf the second time and does not return the third time. Noah removes the ship's covering and sees dry ground, and God tells him to leave the ship with his wife, sons, sons' wives, and all the living creatures. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings of clean animals and birds, and the LORD, pleased by the aroma, resolves never again to curse the ground or strike every living thing, promising that seasons and day and night will continue.

Noah sends out a raven and then a dove three times to learn whether the waters have abated, and he knows they have when the dove returns with an olive leaf. After removing the ship's covering and seeing dry ground, he obeys God's command to leave the ship with his family and the animals. He builds an altar to the LORD and offers burnt offerings of every clean animal and clean bird.

God remembers Noah and the animals, makes a wind pass over the earth, and stops the sources of the waters. He commands Noah to leave the ship and bring out every living thing so they may breed and multiply. The LORD smells the pleasing aroma of Noah's offerings and resolves not to curse the ground or strike every living thing again.

The ship comes to rest on Ararat's mountains on the seventeenth day of the seventh month. Noah opens its window to send out birds and later removes its covering to see dry ground. Everyone and everything aboard goes out of it at God's command.

l: dove (sent out by Noah), Genesis, Chapter 8
s: Noah sends the dove out to see whether the waters have abated, and the first time she finds no place to rest her foot and returns, so Noah takes her back into the ship. Seven days later she returns at evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her mouth. After another seven days Noah sends her out again and she does not return.

The waters subside after God sends a wind over the earth and the deep's fountains and the sky's windows are stopped and the rain restrained. They recede continually, with the mountain tops visible in the tenth month, and are dried up from the earth by the first day of the first month of Noah's six hundred first year. The earth is dry by the twenty-seventh day of the second month.

l: animals and livestock (with Noah), Genesis, Chapter 8
s: God remembers the animals and livestock along with Noah in the ship. At God's command every animal, creeping thing, and bird goes out of the ship after their families, so that they may breed abundantly, be fruitful, and multiply on the earth. Clean animals and birds are taken by Noah for burnt offerings.

The earth is covered by waters at first, then emerges as a wind passes over it, with the mountain tops visible in the tenth month and the ground dry by the second month of the following year. The living creatures from the ship go out onto it to breed and multiply. God declares that while the earth remains, seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, and day and night will not cease.

l: God's promise not to curse the ground again, Genesis, Chapter 8
s: After smelling the pleasing aroma of Noah's offerings, the LORD says in his heart that he will not again curse the ground for man's sake, because the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth. He also says he will never again strike every living thing as he has done. He adds that while the earth remains, seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, and day and night will not cease.

God blesses Noah and his sons, tells them to multiply, gives them every moving living thing for food except flesh with its blood, and declares that anyone who sheds man's blood will have his own blood shed. God then establishes a covenant with Noah, his offspring, and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets his rainbow in the cloud as the sign. The sons of Noah who left the ship are named as Shem, Ham, and Japheth, with Ham the father of Canaan. Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk, and is uncovered in his tent; Ham sees this and tells his brothers, while Shem and Japheth cover their father walking backwards. Noah, on waking, curses Canaan to be a servant of servants, blesses the God of Shem, and asks that God enlarge Japheth, then lives 350 years after the flood and dies at 950.

God blesses Noah and his sons, commands them to be fruitful and multiply, and gives them every moving living thing as food, forbidding the eating of flesh with its blood. He declares he will require an accounting for human life, establishes a covenant with Noah, his offspring and every living creature, and sets the rainbow as its sign.

Noah is blessed by God and receives the covenant along with his sons and descendants. He becomes a farmer, plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered in his tent, then on waking curses Canaan, blesses the God of Shem, and asks that Japheth be enlarged. He lives 350 years after the flood and dies at age 950.

Shem is named as one of Noah's sons who left the ship. Along with Japheth, he covers his father's nakedness with a garment, walking in backwards so as not to see it, and Noah blesses the LORD as the God of Shem and says Japheth will dwell in Shem's tents.
Ham is named as one of Noah's sons and as the father of Canaan. He sees his father's nakedness and tells his two brothers outside, and Noah is said to know what his youngest son had done to him.

Japheth is named as one of Noah's sons who left the ship. With Shem, he covers his father with a garment while facing backwards, and Noah says God will enlarge Japheth, who will dwell in the tents of Shem, with Canaan as his servant.
Canaan is identified as the son of Ham. Noah curses him, saying he will be a servant of servants to his brothers, and twice says Canaan will be the servant of Shem and of Japheth.

l: covenant (God's covenant with Noah, his offspring, and every living creature), Genesis, Chapter 9
s: God establishes his covenant with Noah, his offspring, and every living creature that left the ship, promising that all flesh will never again be cut off by the waters of a flood. He calls it an everlasting covenant for perpetual generations, with the rainbow as its token.

l: rainbow (sign of God's covenant), Genesis, Chapter 9
s: God sets his rainbow in the cloud as the sign of the covenant between him and the earth. When it appears in the cloud, God says he will look at it and remember the everlasting covenant with every living creature.
The flood is referred to as the event that cut off flesh by water, and God promises it will never happen again to destroy the earth. Noah is also said to live 350 years after the flood.

Chapter 10 gives the genealogy of the sons of Noah (Shem, Ham, and Japheth), whose descendants were born after the flood. It lists the sons of Japheth, then of Ham, then of Shem, with notes on their lands, languages, and families. Among Ham's descendants, Cush's son Nimrod is singled out as a mighty hunter before the LORD who founded a kingdom beginning at Babel in Shinar and went on to build Nineveh and other cities in Assyria. Among Shem's descendants, Eber's son Peleg is named for the earth being divided in his days, and Joktan's sons are listed with their dwelling place. The chapter ends by stating that the nations divided from the families of Noah's sons on the earth after the flood.

Noah is named as the father whose three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, had sons born to them after the flood. The chapter closes by calling the listed groups the families of the sons of Noah, from whom the nations divided.

Shem is called the elder brother of Japheth and the father of all the children of Eber. His sons were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram, and his descendants are listed with their families, languages, lands, and nations.

Ham's sons were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan, and the chapter traces the descendants of each. His line is summarized as sons by their families, languages, lands, and nations, and the Canaanite border is described from Sidon toward Gerar to Gaza and toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim to Lasha.

Japheth's sons were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. Gomer's sons and Javan's sons are also listed, and from these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each by language, family, and nation.

Nimrod, son of Cush, began to be a mighty one on the earth and was a mighty hunter before the LORD, which gave rise to a saying. His kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in Shinar, and he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir, Calah, and Resen.

The sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, are the source of the genealogy in this chapter, with their descendants listed in turn. Their families are summed up as the ones from whom the nations divided on the earth after the flood.

l: division of the nations, Genesis, Chapter 10
s: The division is described as the islands of the nations being divided in their lands by language, family, and nation, and each line of Japheth, Ham, and Shem is closed with similar wording. Peleg, a son of Eber, was named for the earth being divided in his days, and the chapter ends stating that the nations divided from Noah's sons' families after the flood.

The people of the whole earth, sharing one language, settle on a plain in Shinar and build bricks to construct a city and a tower reaching the sky so they can make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. The LORD comes down, confuses their language, and scatters them over the earth, so the city is called Babel. The chapter then gives the generations of Shem down through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, and Nahor to Terah, who fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran, father of Lot, dies in Ur of the Chaldees, and Abram marries Sarai, who is barren. Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur toward Canaan, but they settle in Haran, where Terah dies at 205.

The LORD comes down to see the city and tower the people are building, and decides to go down and confuse their language so they cannot understand one another. He scatters them over the surface of all the earth and the building stops.

l: people of the earth (builders of Babel), Genesis, Chapter 11
s: Speaking one language, they travel east, settle in a plain in Shinar, and make bricks to build a city and a tower to the sky, wanting to make a name for themselves and not be scattered. The LORD confuses their language and scatters them across the earth, and they stop building the city.
Babel is the name given to the city the people were building, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. From there the LORD scattered the people over the whole earth.

The people plan the tower with its top reaching to the sky, built of burnt brick with tar for mortar, alongside the city. The LORD comes down to see it, and the building is stopped when he confuses their language and scatters them.

l: language of all the earth, Genesis, Chapter 11
s: At the start of the chapter the whole earth has one language and one speech. The LORD confuses it so people cannot understand one another's speech, which leads to their scattering.

Terah is born in the line of Shem through Nahor, lives seventy years and fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran. After Haran dies in Ur of the Chaldees, Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai toward Canaan, but they stop and live in Haran, where he dies at 205 years old.
Abram is a son of Terah, brother of Nahor and Haran, and uncle of Lot. He marries Sarai and travels with his father from Ur of the Chaldees toward Canaan, stopping in Haran.
Lot is the son of Haran, whose father dies in Ur of the Chaldees while Terah is still alive. His grandfather Terah takes him from Ur toward Canaan, and they settle in Haran.
Sarai is the wife of Abram and is barren, having no child. She goes with Terah, Abram, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldees toward Canaan and lives in Haran.

The LORD tells Abram to leave his country and relatives for a land he will be shown, promising to make him a great nation and bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram, seventy-five years old, departs Haran with his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and their possessions and people, and enters Canaan, where he builds altars at Shechem and near Bethel. A severe famine drives Abram to Egypt, where he asks Sarai to say she is his sister out of fear that the Egyptians will kill him. Pharaoh takes Sarai into his house and treats Abram well, but the LORD afflicts Pharaoh and his house with plagues. Pharaoh confronts Abram, returns Sarai, and has men escort Abram away with his wife and all he has.

Abram obeys the LORD's command, leaving Haran at age seventy-five with Sarai, Lot, and his possessions, and travels through Canaan, building altars and calling on the LORD's name. During the famine he goes to Egypt, where out of fear he asks Sarai to say she is his sister, and he gains livestock and servants because of her. After Pharaoh learns the truth, Abram is rebuked and escorted away with his wife and all that he has.

The LORD commands Abram to go to a land he will show him, promises him a great nation and blessing, and appears to him to promise the land to his offspring. He afflicts Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai.

Sarai, Abram's wife, goes with him from Haran to Canaan and then to Egypt. Abram asks her to say she is his sister because she is beautiful; she is taken into Pharaoh's house, and the LORD sends plagues because of her. Pharaoh then returns her to Abram.

Pharaoh takes Sarai into his house after his princes praise her and deals well with Abram for her sake. After the LORD afflicts him and his house with plagues, he rebukes Abram for not saying she was his wife, tells him to take her and go, and commands men to escort Abram away.
Abram fears the Egyptians will kill him and keep Sarai alive when they see her. Some Egyptians do see that she is very beautiful, and Pharaoh's princes praise her to Pharaoh.

Egypt is where Abram goes to live as a foreigner because of the severe famine. There Sarai is taken into Pharaoh's house, Pharaoh's house is plagued, and Abram is sent away with his wife and possessions.

Abram, Sarai, and Lot enter the land of Canaan, where Canaanites are living at that time. Abram passes through to Shechem and the oak of Moreh, then to the mountain east of Bethel, and travels on toward the South.
A severe famine strikes the land and causes Abram to go down into Egypt to live as a foreigner. It sets in motion the episode involving Sarai and Pharaoh.

l: promise of the land and blessing, Genesis, Chapter 12
s: The LORD promises Abram a great nation, a great name, blessing for those who bless him and a curse for those who treat him with contempt, and blessing for all the families of the earth through him. At Shechem he also promises to give the land to Abram's offspring, and Abram builds an altar in response.

Abram leaves Egypt with his wife, Lot, and all his possessions, returning to the South and then to the altar between Bethel and Ai, where he calls on the LORD's name. Because both Abram and Lot have such great livestock holdings, the land cannot support them together, and strife breaks out between their herdsmen. Abram proposes that they separate, offering Lot first choice of direction, and Lot chooses the well-watered Plain of the Jordan and moves his tent toward Sodom, whose men are described as exceedingly wicked. After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to look in every direction, promising him all the land he sees and offspring as numerous as the dust of the earth. Abram then moves his tent to the oaks of Mamre in Hebron and builds an altar to the LORD there.

Abram returns from Egypt very rich in livestock, silver, and gold, and goes back to the altar he had made earlier between Bethel and Ai, where he calls on the LORD's name. He resolves the strife with Lot by offering him first choice of land and taking the opposite direction, then lives in Canaan. After the LORD promises him the land and countless offspring, he settles by the oaks of Mamre in Hebron and builds an altar there.

Lot travels with Abram out of Egypt and has his own flocks, herds, and tents. When Abram offers him the choice of land, he sees the well-watered Plain of the Jordan, chooses it, travels east, and separates from Abram. He lives in the cities of the plain and moves his tent as far as Sodom.

The LORD is the one whose name Abram calls on at the altar near Bethel and Ai. After Lot separates from Abram, he tells Abram to look in all four directions and promises to give him and his offspring all the land he sees forever. He also promises to make Abram's offspring as countless as the dust of the earth, and Abram builds him an altar at Hebron. The text also notes that the LORD later destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, and that the men of Sodom were sinners against him.

l: strife between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen, Genesis, Chapter 13
s: Strife arises between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and those of Lot's because the land cannot support both men's great possessions together. The Canaanites and Perizzites were living in the land at the time. Abram cites it as the reason for proposing that he and Lot separate, and the separation follows.

l: Plain of the Jordan, Genesis, Chapter 13
s: Lot sees that the whole Plain of the Jordan is well-watered everywhere, like the garden of the LORD and like the land of Egypt, as one goes toward Zoar. The text notes this was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot chooses it for himself, and the cities of the plain become his home.

Lot moves his tent as far as Sodom, one of the cities of the plain. The text describes the men of Sodom as exceedingly wicked and sinners against the LORD, and mentions that the LORD would later destroy Sodom and Gomorrah.

Abram lives in the land of Canaan after Lot separates from him and goes to the cities of the plain. The Canaanites and Perizzites are said to be living in the land at that time. The LORD promises Abram and his offspring all the land he can see, and tells him to walk through it in its length and width.

The LORD promises that Abram's offspring will inherit all the land Abram sees, forever. He also promises to make them as numerous as the dust of the earth, so that they could be counted only if the dust could be counted.

Four kings led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, along with Amraphel, Arioch, and Tidal, fought five kings of the Salt Sea cities, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah, who had rebelled after twelve years of serving Chedorlaomer. The four kings won in the valley of Siddim, took the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and carried off Lot, Abram's brother's son. Abram, living by the oaks of Mamre, led 318 trained men from his house, pursued the captors as far as Dan and Hobah, struck them by night, and brought back Lot, the goods, the women, and the other people. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought out bread and wine and blessed Abram, who gave him a tenth of all. The king of Sodom offered Abram the goods, but Abram refused to take anything of his, except what the young men had eaten and the portion of his allies Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre.

Abram, called the Hebrew, lived by the oaks of Mamre and was allied with Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner. On hearing that his relative Lot was captured, he led 318 trained men born in his house, pursued the captors to Dan and Hobah, struck them by night, and recovered Lot, the goods, the women, and the people. He was blessed by Melchizedek, gave him a tenth of all, and swore by the LORD, God Most High, to take nothing from the king of Sodom, though he allowed his allies and the young men their portion.
Lot, Abram's brother's son, lived in Sodom and was taken captive with his goods by the four kings when they took Sodom's possessions. Abram rescued him and brought back both Lot and his goods.

Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, was served for twelve years by the five kings, who rebelled in the thirteenth year. In the fourteenth year he and his allied kings struck the Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim, Horites, Amalekites, and Amorites, then defeated the five kings in the valley of Siddim. He and the kings with him were afterward slaughtered by Abram's pursuit.

Bera, king of Sodom, joined the four-versus-five battle in the valley of Siddim and fled when the tar pits claimed some of his men. After Abram's victory he met Abram in the King's Valley and asked him to give back the people and keep the goods. Abram refused to take anything of his beyond what the young men had eaten and his allies' portion.

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought out bread and wine to Abram after the victory. He blessed Abram in the name of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, and received a tenth of all from Abram.

God Most High is described as possessor of heaven and earth and is credited by Melchizedek with delivering Abram's enemies into his hand. Abram also identifies the LORD with God Most High when he swears his oath not to take anything from the king of Sodom.

Sodom's king and the kings of Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela rebelled against Chedorlaomer and were defeated in the valley of Siddim. Its goods and food were taken by the victors, and Lot, who lived there, was carried off. Its goods and people were later recovered by Abram, though its king let Abram keep the goods.

l: war of the four kings against the five, Genesis, Chapter 14
s: Amraphel, Arioch, Chedorlaomer, and Tidal fought Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shinab of Admah, Shemeber of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela in the valley of Siddim, full of tar pits, after the five rebelled in the thirteenth year of service. The five kings fled, some falling in the pits and the rest escaping to the hills, and the four kings took the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah and captured Lot. Abram's night pursuit afterward reversed the outcome by recovering the captives and goods.

In a vision, the LORD tells Abram not to be afraid and calls himself Abram's shield and great reward. Abram laments that he is childless and that Eliezer of Damascus, a member of his house, would be his heir, but the LORD says Abram's own son will inherit and shows him the stars as a picture of his offspring. Abram believes, and it is credited to him as righteousness. When Abram asks how he will know he will inherit the land, the LORD has him bring and divide animals and birds, and as a deep sleep and terror fall on Abram, the LORD foretells four hundred years of foreign servitude for his offspring before they come out with great wealth. A smoking furnace and flaming torch pass between the pieces, and the LORD makes a covenant giving Abram's offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, naming the peoples living there.

The LORD comes to Abram in a vision, calling himself Abram's shield and exceedingly great reward, and promises that Abram's own offspring will be his heir, as many as the stars. He identifies himself as the one who brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldees, instructs him in the animal offering, foretells the servitude and deliverance of Abram's offspring and judgment on the nation they serve, and makes a covenant giving the land.

Abram is told not to be afraid, complains that he is childless with Eliezer of Damascus as his heir, and is promised an heir from his own body. He believes the LORD, which is credited to him as righteousness, then asks how he will know he will inherit the land. He prepares and divides the animals, drives away birds of prey, falls into a deep sleep with terror and darkness, and is told he will go to his fathers in peace and be buried at a good old age.

Abram's offspring are promised to be as countless as the stars, with the heir coming from Abram's own body. They will live as foreigners in a land not theirs, serve and be afflicted for four hundred years, then come out with great wealth after the LORD judges that nation, and return in the fourth generation.

The LORD says he brought Abram out of Ur to give him this land to inherit. It is declared given to Abram's offspring, from the river of Egypt to the river Euphrates, and is occupied by the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaim, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites. Its possession awaits the fourth generation, because the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.

After the animals are divided and Abram sleeps, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch pass between the pieces at dark. On that day the LORD makes a covenant with Abram, declaring that he has given the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates to Abram's offspring.

Sarai, Abram's wife, has borne no children, so after Abram has lived ten years in Canaan she gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to him as a wife. Hagar conceives and despises Sarai, and Sarai blames Abram; he tells her Hagar is in her hand, and Sarai deals harshly with Hagar, who flees. The LORD's angel finds Hagar by a fountain on the way to Shur, tells her to return and submit to Sarai, and promises to multiply her offspring. He says she will bear a son named Ishmael, who will be like a wild donkey among men. Hagar names the LORD 'a God who sees,' the well is called Beer Lahai Roi, and Hagar bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.

Sarai, Abram's wife, is childless and says the LORD has restrained her from bearing, so she gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife. When Hagar despises her, Sarai blames Abram, asks the LORD to judge between them, and then deals harshly with Hagar, who flees from her.

Abram listens to Sarai and goes in to Hagar, who conceives. When Sarai complains, he tells her Hagar is in her hand to treat as she sees fit, and he names the son Ishmael when Hagar bears him at age eighty-six.

Hagar, Sarai's Egyptian servant, is given to Abram as a wife and conceives, then looks down on Sarai and flees after Sarai's harsh treatment. The LORD's angel finds her by a fountain on the way to Shur, tells her to return and submit, and promises numerous offspring. She names the LORD 'a God who sees,' and bears Abram a son, Ishmael.

Ishmael is announced by the LORD's angel as the son Hagar will bear, named because the LORD has heard her affliction. He is foretold to be like a wild donkey among men, with his hand against every man and every man's hand against him, living opposed to all his brothers. He is born to Hagar and named by Abram when Abram is eighty-six.

The LORD is said by Sarai to have restrained her from bearing, and she asks him to judge between her and Abram. He has heard Hagar's affliction, and Hagar names him 'a God who sees' after he speaks to her.

When Abram is ninety-nine, God Almighty appears to him and establishes an everlasting covenant, renaming him Abraham and promising him many nations, kings, and the land of Canaan. God commands that every male in Abraham's line and household be circumcised at eight days old as the sign of the covenant, on penalty of being cut off. God also renames Sarai as Sarah and promises that she will bear a son, Isaac, with whom the covenant will be established, while Abraham laughs in disbelief and pleads for Ishmael. God promises to bless Ishmael as well, and Abraham circumcises himself, Ishmael, and all the males of his house on the same day.

Abraham, formerly Abram, is ninety-nine when God appears to him, renames him, and promises he will be father of a multitude of nations. He falls on his face, laughs and doubts that a child can be born to a hundred-year-old man, and asks that Ishmael might live before God. He obeys the command on the same day by circumcising himself, Ishmael, and all the males of his house.

God, identifying himself as God Almighty, establishes his everlasting covenant with Abraham, changes the names of Abram and Sarai, and commands circumcision as the sign. He promises Abraham a son by Sarah named Isaac, declares that the covenant will be established with Isaac, and says he has heard Abraham about Ishmael and will bless him. After finishing his talk, God goes up from Abraham.

Sarai, Abraham's wife, is renamed Sarah by God. God promises to bless her and to give Abraham a son by her, and says she will be a mother of nations from whom kings of peoples will come. Abraham notes that she is ninety years old, and God says she will bear Isaac at the set time next year.

Ishmael is Abraham's son, for whom Abraham pleads that he might live before God. God says the covenant will not be with him but with Isaac, yet promises to bless him, make him fruitful, and make him father of twelve princes and a great nation. He is circumcised at age thirteen on the same day as Abraham.

Isaac is the name God tells Abraham to give to the son Sarah will bear to him at the set time next year. God says he will establish his everlasting covenant with Isaac and with Isaac's offspring after him.

l: covenant (God's covenant with Abraham), Genesis, Chapter 17
s: God declares his covenant with Abraham and his offspring to be everlasting, promising to multiply Abraham, make him father of nations with kings among them, be their God, and give them all the land of Canaan. Abraham and his offspring are to keep it, and it is to be in their flesh. God says it will be established specifically with Isaac, and that anyone uncircumcised has broken it.

l: circumcision (sign of the covenant), Genesis, Chapter 17
s: God commands that every male be circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin as a token of the covenant, at eight days old, including those born in the house or bought from foreigners. An uncircumcised male is to be cut off from his people for breaking the covenant. Abraham, aged ninety-nine, and Ishmael, aged thirteen, are circumcised on the same day along with all the men of the house.

God promises that Abraham's offspring after him, throughout their generations, will share in the everlasting covenant, with God being their God and the land of Canaan their everlasting possession. They are to keep the covenant by circumcising every male. Nations and kings are promised to come from Abraham, and the covenant line is specified as running through Isaac.

Every male in Abraham's household, whether born in the house or bought with money from a foreigner, is included in the circumcision command even if not of his offspring. Abraham circumcises all of them on the same day as God had said. All the men of his house are circumcised with him.

The LORD appears to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre in the form of three men, and Abraham hospitably runs to feed them with bread, cakes, a calf, butter, and milk. The visitors announce that Sarah will have a son in a year; Sarah, listening from the tent, laughs to herself, then denies it out of fear, and is told she did laugh. The LORD reflects on Abraham's calling to become a great nation and reveals that the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin grievous, so he will go down to see. Abraham stays before the LORD and bargains for Sodom, asking whether he will spare the city for fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten righteous people, and the LORD agrees each time before departing.

Abraham welcomes the three men with eager hospitality, hurrying to have bread, cakes, and a calf prepared and standing by them as they eat. He walks with them on their way, and the LORD reveals that he has chosen Abraham to become a great nation and to command his household to keep the way of the LORD. Abraham then stays before the LORD and pleads for Sodom.

Sarah is told to make cakes from three seahs of fine meal and overhears from the tent door that she will have a son. Being old and past childbearing, she laughs within herself, then denies laughing out of fear and is told, "No, but you did laugh."

The LORD appears to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, knows that Sarah laughed, and asks, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" He declares he will return at the set time and that Sarah will have a son. He also says he will go down to see whether the deeds of Sodom and Gomorrah match the reports, and agrees to spare Sodom for ten righteous, then goes his way.

Three men stand near Abraham as he sits at his tent door. He bows, washes-their-feet hospitality is offered, and they eat and agree to stay. They ask about Sarah, announce that she will have a son, then rise and look toward Sodom. Two of them go toward Sodom while Abraham remains before the LORD.

The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is said to be great and their sin very grievous. The LORD says he will go down to see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports. Men go toward the city, and the LORD agrees to spare it for the sake of as few as ten righteous.

Abraham asks whether the LORD will consume the righteous with the wicked. The LORD agrees to spare the whole place for fifty, then forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten righteous found within it. The text does not say whether any are found.

l: Sarah's laughter and denial, Genesis, Chapter 18
s: Sarah laughs within herself, wondering whether she will have pleasure now that she and her lord are old. The LORD repeats her words to Abraham and asks why she laughed. She denies it, afraid, and is told that she did laugh.

l: Abraham's intercession for Sodom, Genesis, Chapter 18
s: Abraham comes near and appeals to the Judge of all the earth to do right and not kill the righteous with the wicked. He acknowledges he is dust and ashes and lowers the number step by step from fifty to ten, twice asking that the Lord not be angry. The LORD grants each request, then goes his way, and Abraham returns to his place.

l: destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Genesis, Chapter 18
s: The destruction of Sodom is under consideration but not carried out in this unit. The LORD says he will go down to see whether the reports are true, and he promises not to destroy the city for the sake of ten righteous.

The visitors say that Sarah will have a son at about this time next year. The LORD repeats the promise after Sarah laughs, saying that at the set time, when the season comes around, Sarah will have a son. The narrator notes that Abraham and Sarah are old and she is past the age of childbearing.

Two angels come to Sodom in the evening, and Lot welcomes them into his house. The men of Sodom surround the house demanding the visitors, Lot offers his two virgin daughters instead, and the angels strike the crowd with blindness and tell Lot to flee. At dawn the angels lead Lot, his wife, and his two daughters out; Lot is allowed to take refuge in Zoar, the LORD rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Abraham sees the smoke the next morning, and God remembers him in saving Lot. Lot then lives in a cave with his daughters, who get him drunk and lie with him to preserve the family line, bearing Moab and Ben Ammi, the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

Lot sits in the gate of Sodom, bows to the two angels, and urges them into his house, where he feeds them. He offers his two virgin daughters to the crowd to protect his guests, and is pulled inside by the angels. He lingers when told to flee, is led out by the hand, pleads to go to the small city of Zoar instead of the mountains, and later moves to a cave in the mountain with his daughters. There his daughters get him drunk and lie with him, and he does not know when they lie down or get up.

The two angels come to Sodom at evening, at first say they will stay in the street, then go home with Lot and eat his feast. They pull Lot inside, strike the crowd with blindness, and announce that they are sent to destroy the city. They hurry Lot, his wife, and his daughters out by the hand, set them outside the city, and agree to spare Zoar.

Sodom is the city where Lot lives and where its men surround his house demanding to have sex with his guests. The angels say the outcry against it has grown so great before the LORD that it will be destroyed. It is overthrown with sulfur and fire from the sky, with Gomorrah, the whole plain, and all its inhabitants.

The men of Sodom, young and old from every quarter, surround Lot's house and demand that he bring out his guests so they can have sex with them. They reject Lot's offer of his daughters, call him a foreigner who appoints himself judge, threaten to deal worse with him, and press to break the door. The angels strike them with blindness so that they weary themselves trying to find the door.

The LORD is said to have been sent the outcry against Sodom, which has grown great before him, and he sends the angels to destroy it. He is merciful to Lot, and he rains sulfur and fire from the sky on Sodom and Gomorrah. God remembers Abraham and sends Lot out of the middle of the overthrow.

Zoar is the small nearby city that Lot asks to flee to instead of the mountains. The angel grants this request and does not overthrow it, and the city is named Zoar. Lot reaches it as the sun rises, but later leaves it because he is afraid to live there.
Lot's wife is taken by the hand and led out of Sodom by the angels along with Lot and their two daughters. She looks back from behind him and becomes a pillar of salt.

Lot's two virgin daughters are offered by Lot to the men of Sodom, who do not take them. They are led out of the city with their parents and live with Lot in a cave in the mountain. Both become pregnant by their father and bear sons.

The firstborn proposes to her younger sister that they make their father drink wine and lie with him to preserve the family line, since no man is left to come in to them. She lies with Lot the first night and bears a son named Moab.
The younger daughter is urged by her sister to join the plan and lies with Lot the second night after they make him drink wine. She bears a son named Ben Ammi.

Abraham goes up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD and looks toward Sodom and Gomorrah. He sees smoke rising like the smoke of a furnace. God remembers Abraham and, for that reason, sends Lot out of the overthrow.
Moab is the son born to Lot's firstborn daughter by her father. He is named as the father of the Moabites to this day.
Ben Ammi is the son born to Lot's younger daughter by her father. He is named as the father of the children of Ammon to this day.

l: destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Genesis, Chapter 19
s: The angels announce the coming destruction because the outcry against the cities has grown great before the LORD. After Lot reaches Zoar, the LORD rains sulfur and fire from the sky, overthrowing the cities, all the plain, their inhabitants, and what grew on the ground. Abraham sees the smoke rising like a furnace the next morning.

l: incest of Lot's daughters with Lot, Genesis, Chapter 19
s: Believing no man is left on earth to come in to them, Lot's daughters plan to preserve their father's family line. On two successive nights they make him drink wine, and first the firstborn and then the younger lies with him, without his knowing when they lie down or rise. Both become pregnant and bear Moab and Ben Ammi.

Abraham moves to the land of the South and lives as a foreigner in Gerar, where he says his wife Sarah is his sister. Abimelech, king of Gerar, takes Sarah, but God warns him in a dream that he is a dead man because she is a married woman. Abimelech, who had not approached her, protests his innocence, and God confirms this, tells him to restore her, and says Abraham as a prophet will pray for him. Abimelech confronts Abraham, who explains that he feared there was no fear of God in Gerar and that Sarah is his father's daughter and half-sister. Abimelech returns Sarah with livestock, servants, and a thousand pieces of silver, Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech's household, whose wombs He had closed because of Sarah.

Abraham settles as a foreigner in Gerar and tells people Sarah is his sister, fearing he will be killed for his wife. He explains to Abimelech that she is his father's daughter and that he had asked her to say this everywhere they went. He receives livestock, servants, silver, and Sarah back, and God, who calls him a prophet, heals Abimelech's household through his prayer.

Sarah is taken by Abimelech after Abraham calls her his sister, but Abimelech does not come near her. She is restored to Abraham, and Abimelech tells her that the thousand pieces of silver given to her brother is a covering of the eyes and that she is vindicated before all. It is learned that she is Abraham's half-sister, the daughter of his father but not his mother, and that she said of him, 'He is my brother.'

Abimelech, king of Gerar, takes Sarah, is warned by God in a dream, and pleads that he acted in the integrity of his heart. He obeys by restoring Sarah, rebukes Abraham, gives him sheep, cattle, servants, a thousand pieces of silver, and the freedom to dwell in his land. After Abraham prays, God heals him, his wife, and his female servants, and they bear children.

God comes to Abimelech in a dream, declares him a dead man for taking a married woman, and says He kept Abimelech from sinning by not letting him touch her. He commands her return, names Abraham a prophet who will pray for Abimelech, and warns of death for Abimelech and all his people if he refuses. After Abraham prays, God heals Abimelech's household, having closed all their wombs because of Sarah.

Abraham's statement that Sarah is his sister, which she echoes by calling him her brother, leads Abimelech to take her. Abraham explains that he feared being killed for his wife and that she is truly his father's daughter, and that he had asked her to say it everywhere they traveled. Abimelech calls it a great sin brought on him and his kingdom, yet it ends with Sarah restored and Abraham enriched.

God fulfills his promise to Sarah, who bears Abraham a son, Isaac, when Abraham is one hundred years old; Abraham circumcises him at eight days and holds a great feast when he is weaned. Sarah sees Hagar's son mocking and demands that Abraham cast out Hagar and her son. God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah and promises to make a nation of the servant's son too, so Abraham sends Hagar away with bread and water. In the wilderness of Beersheba, when the water runs out, God hears the boy's voice, the angel of God speaks to Hagar, and God opens her eyes to a well; the boy grows up as an archer in the wilderness of Paran. Abimelech and Phicol ask Abraham to swear fair dealing, Abraham complains about a seized well, and the two make a covenant at Beersheba, sealed with seven ewe lambs, after which Abraham plants a tamarisk tree and calls on the LORD, the Everlasting God.

Sarah conceives and bears Abraham a son in his old age, as God had spoken, and says God has made her laugh. After seeing Hagar's son mocking, she tells Abraham to cast out the servant and her son so that he will not be heir with Isaac.

Abraham names his son Isaac, circumcises him at eight days, and is one hundred years old at his birth. Though grieved, he obeys God's word, sending Hagar and the child away with bread and water, and later complains to Abimelech about a seized well, makes a covenant with him, plants a tamarisk tree at Beersheba, and calls on the LORD, the Everlasting God.

Isaac is born to Sarah and Abraham at the set time God had spoken of, and is circumcised at eight days. He grows and is weaned, and Abraham holds a great feast that day. God says Abraham's offspring will be named through him.

God fulfills his word to Sarah and Abraham by giving them Isaac. He tells Abraham to listen to Sarah and promises to make a nation of Hagar's son too, then hears the boy's voice, opens Hagar's eyes to a well, and is with the boy as he grows. Abraham calls him the LORD, the Everlasting God.

Hagar, the Egyptian servant, is sent away by Abraham with bread, a container of water, and her child, and wanders in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water is spent she weeps at a distance from the child, and the angel of God tells her not to be afraid; God opens her eyes to a well. She later gets a wife for her son from Egypt.

Hagar's son is seen mocking by Sarah, which leads to his being sent away with his mother. In the wilderness God hears his voice and promises to make him a great nation; he is given water from the well, grows up as an archer in the wilderness of Paran, and has a wife from Egypt.

Abimelech, with Phicol the captain of his army, asks Abraham to swear not to deal falsely with him or his descendants, noting that God is with Abraham. He says he did not know who seized the well, and makes a covenant with Abraham before returning to the land of the Philistines.

Beersheba is the wilderness where Hagar wanders after being sent away. Abraham names the place because he and Abimelech swore an oath there, and it is where they made a covenant; Abraham plants a tamarisk tree there and calls on the LORD.

l: well (Abraham's well at Beersheba), Genesis, Chapter 21
s: Abraham complains that Abimelech's servants violently took away a water well. Abimelech says he knew nothing of it, and Abraham gives seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug this well.
Abraham sets seven ewe lambs of the flock apart by themselves. He tells Abimelech to take them from his hand as a witness that Abraham dug the well.

After Abimelech asks for an oath of fair dealing, Abraham agrees to swear, gives sheep and cattle to Abimelech, and the two make a covenant. It is made at Beersheba, which is named for the oath both swore there.

God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer his only son Isaac as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah. Abraham obeys, travels three days with Isaac and two young men, binds Isaac on an altar, and takes up the knife. The LORD's angel stops him from the sky, and Abraham offers a ram caught in the thicket instead, naming the place "The LORD Will Provide." The angel then repeats God's oath to bless Abraham greatly, multiply his offspring, and bless all nations through them. Abraham returns to Beersheba, and he is told of the children born to his brother Nahor by Milcah and by his concubine Reumah, including Bethuel, father of Rebekah.

Abraham answers God's call with "Here I am," rises early, and carries out the command, traveling to the appointed place, building the altar, binding Isaac, and taking the knife to kill him. Stopped by the LORD's angel, he sacrifices a ram instead, names the place "The LORD Will Provide," and receives an oath of blessing for having obeyed. He then returns to his young men, lives at Beersheba, and is told of the children born to his brother Nahor.

Isaac is called Abraham's only son, whom he loves, and is commanded to be offered as a burnt offering. He carries the wood, asks where the lamb for the offering is, and is bound and laid on the altar by Abraham. He is spared when the angel stops Abraham, and a ram is offered in his place.

God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac and to go to a mountain in Moriah that he will name. Through the angel, he declares that he now knows Abraham fears him because he did not withhold his son. He swears by himself to bless Abraham greatly, multiply his offspring like the stars and the sand, and bless all nations through his offspring.

l: angel of the LORD, Genesis, Chapter 22
s: The LORD's angel calls to Abraham from the sky, telling him not to lay a hand on the boy, because God now knows that Abraham fears him. He calls a second time, speaking the LORD's oath that Abraham will be blessed, his offspring multiplied, and all nations blessed through his offspring because he obeyed.

God commands that Isaac be offered as a burnt offering on a mountain in Moriah, and Abraham brings the wood, fire, and knife for it. When Isaac asks where the lamb is, Abraham says God will provide it. Abraham finally offers a ram as the burnt offering instead of his son.

l: ram (caught in the thicket), Genesis, Chapter 22
s: After the angel stops Abraham, he looks up and sees a ram caught by its horns in the thicket behind him. Abraham takes it and offers it up as a burnt offering instead of his son, and he names the place "The LORD Will Provide."

l: God's testing of Abraham, Genesis, Chapter 22
s: The test begins when God tells Abraham to offer his only son Isaac as a burnt offering, and Abraham obeys without withholding him. It ends when the angel stops him, declaring that God now knows Abraham fears him. The test is followed by the oath of blessing given because Abraham obeyed God's voice.

Sarah dies at age 127 in Kiriath Arba (Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham mourns and weeps for her. Calling himself a stranger and foreigner, Abraham asks the children of Heth for a burying-place, and they offer him their best tombs. Abraham asks them to intercede with Ephron the son of Zohar to sell him the cave of Machpelah at the end of Ephron's field. Ephron offers to give the field and cave outright, but Abraham insists on paying, and Ephron names a price of four hundred shekels of silver. Abraham weighs out the silver in the hearing of the Hittites, the field, cave, and trees are deeded to him, and he buries Sarah in the cave.

Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years and died in Kiriath Arba (Hebron) in the land of Canaan. Abraham mourned and wept for her, and afterward buried her in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre.

Abraham mourned Sarah, then described himself to the children of Heth as a stranger and foreigner and asked for a burying-place. He bowed to the people of the land, insisted on paying full price rather than accept a gift, weighed out four hundred shekels of silver to Ephron, and buried Sarah in the cave.

Ephron the Hittite, sitting among the children of Heth, was asked through them to sell the cave of Machpelah at the end of his field. He first offered to give the field and cave, then, when Abraham insisted on paying, named a price of four hundred shekels of silver, which he received.

The children of Heth received Abraham's request, called him a prince of God among them, and offered him the best of their tombs. Abraham bowed to them and asked them to entreat Ephron; they witnessed the sale at the city gate, and the field and cave were deeded to Abraham in their presence.
Machpelah is the location of Ephron's field and cave, before Mamre (that is, Hebron), in the land of Canaan. Sarah was buried in the cave of the field of Machpelah.

l: cave (Ephron's cave at Machpelah), Genesis, Chapter 23
s: Abraham asked that Ephron sell him the cave of Machpelah, which lay in the end of Ephron's field. It was deeded to Abraham along with the field, and Sarah was buried in it.

Ephron's field in Machpelah, before Mamre, contained the cave and trees within all its borders. Ephron offered it as a gift, but Abraham paid for it, and it was deeded to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the children of Heth.

Abraham asked the children of Heth for a possession of a burying-place so he could bury his dead out of his sight. He obtained it when the field and cave were deeded to him as a possession for a burial place, and Sarah was buried there.

l: silver purchase (Abraham's payment for the field), Genesis, Chapter 23
s: Ephron said the land was worth four hundred shekels of silver between him and Abraham, and Abraham weighed out that amount according to the current merchants' standard. This was done in the hearing of the children of Heth, and the field, cave, and trees were then deeded to Abraham before all who went in at the city gate.

Abraham, old and blessed by the LORD, makes his chief servant swear not to take a Canaanite wife for Isaac but to find one among Abraham's relatives, without taking Isaac back to the old land. The servant travels to the city of Nahor with ten camels and prays at the spring for a sign: the young woman who offers water to him and his camels will be the one appointed for Isaac. Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, does exactly this, and the servant gives her gold gifts and worships the LORD. He tells her family his story, Laban and Bethuel agree that the matter comes from the LORD, and Rebekah consents to go at once. She travels to Isaac, covers herself with her veil when she sees him, and becomes his wife, and Isaac is comforted after his mother's death.

Abraham, old and blessed by the LORD in all things, makes his servant swear to find Isaac a wife from his own relatives and not from the Canaanites, and forbids him to take Isaac back to the old land. He assures the servant that the LORD will send his angel ahead and that the servant will be free of the oath if the woman is unwilling.

Abraham's servant swears the oath, travels to the city of Nahor with ten camels, and prays at the spring for a sign, which Rebekah fulfills. He gives her gold gifts, worships the LORD, tells her family his story, secures their consent, gives gifts to Rebekah and her family, and brings her to Isaac, to whom he reports all he had done.

Isaac is the son for whom a wife is sought and is not to be taken back to Abraham's homeland. He goes out to meditate in the field at evening, sees the camels coming, receives Rebekah into his mother Sarah's tent, takes her as wife, loves her, and is comforted after his mother's death.

Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel and a very beautiful virgin, draws water for the servant and all his camels, answering the sign he prayed for. She receives gold gifts, tells her family what happened, agrees to go with the man when asked, is blessed by her family, and on seeing Isaac covers herself with her veil before becoming his wife.

Laban, Rebekah's brother, runs to the spring after seeing the ring and bracelets and hearing his sister's words. He welcomes the servant into the house and provides for the camels, listens to his message, and with Bethuel says the matter proceeds from the LORD and gives Rebekah to go.

The LORD is invoked as the God of heaven and earth and of Abraham, who is said to have blessed Abraham, spoken to him and sworn to give the land to his offspring. He is credited with answering the servant's prayer and leading him on the way, and Laban and Bethuel say the matter proceeds from him.

l: spring (outside the city of Nahor), Genesis, Chapter 24
s: The spring outside the city of Nahor is where the servant makes his camels kneel at evening, when women come to draw water, and where he prays for a sign. Rebekah draws water there for him and his camels, and Laban comes out to meet the man there.

Abraham makes his servant swear by the LORD, with his hand under Abraham's thigh, not to take a Canaanite wife for Isaac but to find one among Abraham's relatives. The oath releases the servant if the woman is unwilling, though he must not bring Isaac back; the servant repeats its terms to Rebekah's family.

Abraham takes Keturah as another wife, has children by her, gives everything to Isaac, and sends the sons of his concubines east with gifts. He dies at 175 and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah beside Sarah. God blesses Isaac, and the chapter lists the twelve sons of Ishmael and notes that Ishmael died at 137. Isaac marries Rebekah at forty, and after he entreats the LORD for her barrenness she conceives twins and is told the elder will serve the younger. Esau and Jacob are born, and Esau, famished, sells his birthright to Jacob for bread and lentil stew.

Abraham took Keturah as another wife and fathered Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah by her. He gave all he had to Isaac, sent the sons of his concubines eastward with gifts, and died at 175 years old, full of years.

Isaac received all that Abraham had, and after Abraham's death God blessed him and he lived by Beer Lahai Roi. At forty he married Rebekah, entreated the LORD because she was barren, and was sixty when the twins Esau and Jacob were born. He loved Esau because he ate his venison.

Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar the Egyptian, helped Isaac bury Abraham. He fathered twelve sons, listed beginning with Nebaioth and Kedar, who became twelve princes according to their nations. He died at 137 and was gathered to his people.

Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Syrian and sister of Laban, married Isaac and conceived after he entreated the LORD. When the children struggled within her she inquired of the LORD and was told two nations were in her womb and the elder would serve the younger. She bore twins and loved Jacob.

Esau was born first, red all over like a hairy garment, and grew into a skillful hunter and man of the field loved by Isaac. Famished, he asked Jacob for red stew, gaining the name Edom, and swore away his birthright for bread and lentil stew. The text says he despised his birthright.

Jacob was born second, holding Esau's heel, and grew into a quiet man living in tents whom Rebekah loved. He boiled stew and made Esau swear to sell him the birthright before giving Esau bread and lentil stew.

l: Abraham's death and burial, Genesis, Chapter 25
s: Abraham gave up his spirit at a good old age, 175 years, and was gathered to his people. Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the Hittite near Mamre, which Abraham had purchased from the children of Heth, alongside his wife Sarah. After this, God blessed Isaac.

Jacob demanded Esau's birthright in exchange for food, and Esau, saying he was about to die and the birthright was no good to him, swore and sold it. The text concludes that Esau despised his birthright.

l: stew (Jacob's red lentil stew), Genesis, Chapter 25
s: Jacob boiled stew, and Esau came in from the field famished and asked for some of the red stew, which is why he was called Edom. Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew in exchange for his birthright, and Esau ate and drank, rose up, and went his way.

During a famine, Isaac goes to Gerar, where the LORD tells him not to go to Egypt and renews to him the promise made to Abraham. Isaac passes off Rebekah as his sister out of fear, but Abimelech sees them together, rebukes him, and orders that no one touch Isaac or his wife. Isaac prospers greatly, the Philistines envy him, and Abimelech sends him away; he reopens Abraham's wells and digs new ones, naming them Esek, Sitnah, and Rehoboth. At Beersheba the LORD reassures him, and Abimelech comes with Ahuzzath and Phicol to make a covenant, after which Isaac's servants find water and the well is named Shibah. The chapter closes with Esau marrying Judith and Basemath, Hittite women who grieve Isaac and Rebekah.

Isaac goes to Gerar during a famine, is told by the LORD not to go to Egypt, and claims Rebekah is his sister out of fear. He sows and reaps a hundredfold, becomes very great, is sent away by Abimelech, reopens his father's wells, digs new ones, and settles at Beersheba, where he builds an altar and makes a covenant with Abimelech.

Abimelech, king of the Philistines at Gerar, sees Isaac caressing Rebekah, rebukes him for calling her his sister, and commands that anyone who touches Isaac or his wife be put to death. He later tells Isaac to leave because he is mightier, then comes to Beersheba with Ahuzzath and Phicol to seek an oath and covenant, acknowledging that Isaac is blessed by the LORD.

Rebekah is Isaac's wife, whom he calls his sister because she is beautiful and he fears being killed for her. Abimelech sees Isaac caressing her, which reveals the truth, and she and Isaac are later grieved by Esau's Hittite wives.

The LORD appears to Isaac twice, telling him to stay in the land, reaffirming the oath sworn to Abraham, and promising blessing, many offspring, and blessing for all nations through his offspring. He blesses Isaac's harvest and flocks and assures him at Beersheba not to fear, for Abraham's sake.

Abraham is named as the one whose obedience to the LORD's voice, requirements, commandments, statutes, and laws is the reason for the promises to Isaac. His servants had dug wells that the Philistines stopped up after his death, and Isaac restores them under their original names.
The Philistines envy Isaac's flocks, herds, and household. They had stopped and filled with earth the wells dug in Abraham's days, and the herdsmen of Gerar quarrel with Isaac's herdsmen over water.
Gerar is where Isaac goes to Abimelech during the famine and lives for a long time. He later moves to the valley of Gerar, where his servants find a well and its herdsmen contend with his.

Isaac goes up to Beersheba, where the LORD appears to him the same night, and he builds an altar, pitches his tent, and has a well dug. After the oath with Abimelech the well is called Shibah, and the city is named Beersheba to this day.

l: wells (Abraham's and Isaac's wells), Genesis, Chapter 26
s: The wells dug in Abraham's days had been stopped and filled with earth by the Philistines, and Isaac digs them again and gives them their father's names. His servants' new wells are named Esek and Sitnah because of disputes, Rehoboth because there was no argument, and Shibah at Beersheba.

l: covenant (between Isaac and Abimelech), Genesis, Chapter 26
s: Abimelech, Ahuzzath, and Phicol propose an oath and covenant that Isaac will do them no harm, since they saw the LORD was with him and had done him only good. Isaac holds a feast, they swear an oath to one another the next morning, and they depart in peace.

The aged and blind Isaac asks his elder son Esau to hunt venison and prepare savory food so that Isaac can bless him before he dies. Rebekah overhears and directs her younger son Jacob to fetch two young goats, which she cooks, and she dresses him in Esau's clothes and goat skins so he can pose as Esau despite his smooth skin. Jacob deceives Isaac, who is suspicious but is convinced by the hairy hands and the smell of the clothing, and receives the blessing of plenty and lordship over his brothers. When Esau returns, Isaac trembles, confirms that the blessing cannot be undone, and gives Esau a lesser blessing of living by the sword and eventually breaking Jacob's yoke. Esau resolves to kill Jacob after Isaac's death, so Rebekah sends Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran and persuades Isaac with her complaint about the daughters of Heth.

Old and blind, Isaac asks Esau to bring venison and savory food so he can bless him. He questions the person who comes, feels his hands, smells his clothing, and is deceived into blessing Jacob. On learning the truth he trembles violently, affirms that Jacob will be blessed, and gives Esau a lesser blessing of living by the sword and serving his brother until he breaks loose.

Esau, the elder son, goes to hunt venison at Isaac's request but returns to find that Jacob has already taken the blessing. He cries bitterly, begs for a blessing of his own, and receives one of dwelling in fatness of the earth, living by his sword, and serving his brother. He then hates Jacob and resolves in his heart to kill him after Isaac's death.

Jacob, the younger and smooth-skinned son, fears being seen as a deceiver but obeys Rebekah, wears Esau's clothes and goat skins, and tells Isaac he is Esau. He receives Isaac's blessing of plenty, rule over nations and his brothers. Esau's murderous plan then forces him to flee to Laban in Haran at Rebekah's command.

Rebekah overhears Isaac's instructions to Esau and directs Jacob to obtain the blessing, taking on any curse herself. She cooks the goats, dresses Jacob in Esau's clothes and goat skins, and sends him to Isaac. When she learns of Esau's plan to kill Jacob, she sends Jacob to her brother Laban, and she tells Isaac she is weary of life because of the daughters of Heth.
