l: blessing (Isaac's blessing of Jacob), Genesis, Chapter 27
s: Isaac's blessing gives Jacob the dew of the sky, the fatness of the earth, grain and new wine, service from peoples and nations, and lordship over his brothers. It also declares cursed those who curse him and blessed those who bless him. It cannot be reversed once given, leaving Esau only a lesser blessing and provoking his hatred of Jacob.

Isaac asks Esau to hunt venison and make savory food so that his soul may bless him. Rebekah instead prepares savory food from two young goats, as Isaac loves, and Jacob brings it to him with bread. Isaac eats it before Esau arrives with his own.

l: deception of Isaac (Jacob's impersonation of Esau), Genesis, Chapter 27
s: Rebekah plans and Jacob carries out the impersonation using Esau's clothes, goat skins on his hands and neck, and the claim that the LORD gave him quick success. Isaac notes the voice is Jacob's but accepts the hairy hands and the smell of the clothing as Esau's. The deceit is exposed when Esau arrives, and Isaac says Jacob came with deceit.

Isaac blesses Jacob and commands him not to marry a Canaanite woman, sending him to Paddan Aram to take a wife from the daughters of Laban, his mother's brother. Esau, seeing that Canaanite wives displease Isaac, marries Mahalath, a daughter of Ishmael, in addition to his existing wives. On the way from Beersheba toward Haran, Jacob sleeps at a certain place and dreams of a stairway reaching heaven, where the LORD promises him the land, countless offspring, blessing to all families of the earth, and his own presence. Jacob wakes in awe, sets up his stone pillow as a pillar, anoints it with oil, names the place Bethel, and vows that if God keeps and provides for him and brings him home in peace, the LORD will be his God and he will give a tenth of all.

Jacob is blessed and commanded by Isaac not to marry a Canaanite woman, and he obeys his father and mother by going to Paddan Aram. Along the way he dreams of a stairway to heaven and receives the LORD's promises, then sets up his stone as a pillar, names the place Bethel, and makes a vow.

Isaac calls Jacob, blesses him, and commands him not to take a Canaanite wife but to take one from Laban's daughters in Paddan Aram. He prays that God Almighty would make Jacob fruitful and give him the blessing of Abraham and the land, then sends him away. His displeasure with Canaanite daughters prompts Esau's new marriage.

Esau sees that Isaac blessed Jacob, sent him to Paddan Aram, and forbade Canaanite wives, and that Jacob obeyed. Noting that Canaanite women displease his father, he goes to Ishmael and takes Mahalath, Ishmael's daughter and Nebaioth's sister, as a wife in addition to his existing wives.

Isaac invokes God Almighty to bless Jacob. In the dream, the LORD identifies himself as the God of Abraham and Isaac, promises Jacob the land, offspring like the dust, blessing for all families of the earth, and his presence and protection until he fulfills what he has spoken. Jacob afterward vows that the LORD will be his God if these things come to pass.

Paddan Aram is the destination to which Isaac sends Jacob, to the house of Bethuel, Rebekah's father, to take a wife from the daughters of Laban. Laban is described as son of Bethuel the Syrian and brother of Rebekah. Jacob sets out toward it from Beersheba, heading toward Haran.
Bethel is the name Jacob gives to the place where he slept and dreamed, which was formerly called Luz as the name of the city. Jacob declares it none other than God's house and the gate of heaven.
The stairway is set on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascend and descend on it. The LORD stands above it as he speaks to Jacob.

l: stone pillar (Jacob's stone at Bethel), Genesis, Chapter 28
s: Jacob takes one of the stones of the place as his pillow, and in the morning sets it up as a pillar and pours oil on its top. In his vow he says this stone will be God's house.

While sleeping at a certain place after sunset, Jacob dreams of a stairway with angels ascending and descending and the LORD standing above it. The LORD gives promises of land, offspring, blessing and presence. Jacob wakes afraid, recognizing that the LORD is in the place and that it is the gate of heaven.

Jacob vows that if God is with him, keeps him on his way, gives him bread and clothing, and brings him back to his father's house in peace, then the LORD will be his God. The stone pillar will become God's house, and he will give God a tenth of all that he is given.

The LORD promises Jacob the land on which he lies, for him and his offspring, and says he will bring him again into this land. Isaac's blessing likewise speaks of Jacob inheriting the land where he travels, which God gave to Abraham. The offspring are to spread west, east, north, and south.

Jacob travels to the land of the children of the east and meets shepherds at a well, who tell him they are from Haran and know Laban. Rachel, Laban's daughter, arrives with her father's sheep, and Jacob rolls the stone from the well to water them, then weeps and tells her he is her father's relative. Laban welcomes Jacob, and Jacob agrees to serve seven years for Rachel, but Laban gives him Leah in the evening instead, defending this as local custom. Jacob fulfills Leah's week and receives Rachel too, agreeing to serve seven more years, and loves Rachel more than Leah. The LORD sees that Leah is hated and opens her womb, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah while Rachel remains barren.

Jacob journeys to the land of the children of the east, meets Rachel at the well, rolls away the stone to water Laban's flock, and weeps as he kisses her. He serves Laban seven years for Rachel, is given Leah instead, and agrees to serve seven more years to also receive Rachel, whom he loves more than Leah. He fathers Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah with Leah.

Laban, Rebekah's brother and Jacob's mother's brother, welcomes Jacob to his house, calls him his bone and flesh, and offers him wages. He deceives Jacob by bringing Leah to him instead of Rachel, justifying it by saying the younger is not given before the firstborn, and secures seven more years of service from Jacob. He also gives servants Zilpah to Leah and Bilhah to Rachel.

Rachel, Laban's younger daughter, is beautiful in form and attractive, and arrives at the well with her father's sheep, which she keeps. Jacob kisses her and tells her he is Rebekah's son, and she runs to tell her father. Jacob loves her and eventually marries her, but she is barren.

Leah, Laban's elder daughter, has weak eyes and is given to Jacob in the evening in place of Rachel. The LORD sees she is hated and opens her womb, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, interpreting each birth in relation to the LORD and to her hope for her husband's love. After Judah she stops bearing.

The LORD sees that Leah is hated and opens her womb, while Rachel remains barren. Leah credits him with looking at her affliction and hearing that she is hated, and she says she will praise him at Judah's birth.

l: well (in the field where Jacob met Rachel), Genesis, Chapter 29
s: The well in the field is where three flocks of sheep lie waiting to be watered, and its mouth is covered by a large stone. Jacob meets the shepherds and then Rachel here, and he waters Laban's flock from it.

l: stone (on the well's mouth), Genesis, Chapter 29
s: The large stone on the well's mouth is rolled away only when all the flocks are gathered, after which it is put back in its place. Jacob rolls it away himself to water Laban's flock when Rachel arrives.
